claims.text: Intermediate thermal aging induces a transient embrittlement regime in FCC/B2 eutectic HEAs.
Intermediate aging coarsens or otherwise evolves local chemical orders within the B2 phase.
Evolution of local chemical order raises the APB energy of the B2 phase to a critical value.
A sufficiently high APB energy suppresses dislocation cross-slip.
Suppression of cross-slip causes planar slip localization at phase boundaries.
Planar slip localization at phase boundaries produces stress concentrations and brittle fracture.
At higher temperatures, thermal activation overcomes the APB barrier or local chemical orders dissolve, restoring cross-slip and ductility.
The as-cast eutectic HEA has a fine, regular lamellar structure containing FCC and B2 phases.
The FCC constituent is mechanically soft relative to the hard B2-structured ordered constituent.
The as-cast eutectic alloy exhibits unusually high strain hardening because its fine lamellae store dislocations and its B2 regions impede dislocation motion.
The relevant intermediate aging range is approximately 600–800 °C.
The embrittling aging temperatures lie below the B2 solvus and above the onset temperature for significant local chemical order evolution.
Classical impurity-driven grain-boundary embrittlement is absent in the proposed aging regime.
Dislocations entering ordered B2 domains must cut through anti-phase boundaries.
High titanium content can significantly increase APB energy in an ordered precipitate phase.
The ductility minimum should be accompanied by planar slip bands and fracture at phase boundaries.
Impurity segregation and simple grain coarsening do not account for a transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition in the absence of impurities.
At lower temperatures, insufficient local chemical order evolution preserves ductility, whereas at higher temperatures thermal disordering restores ductility.
The temperature window depends on alloy composition and the kinetics associated with B2-stabilizing elements such as Al and Ti.
APB energy can be estimated from dislocation splitting width during microscopy.
